### WHAT IT IS
The **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P., to regulate the functioning and registration of computer training institutes, prescribe syllabus and fee structures, and curb exorbitant fee collection and sudden closures by unregistered centres [42, 44, 45].

### PENAL PROVISIONS: MINIMUM IMPRISONMENT AND FINE
Under **Clause 10** of the Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004, any person who violates the provisions of the Act faces mandatory minimum statutory penalties [64]:

* **Minimum Term of Imprisonment:** Not less than **three years** [64].
* **Minimum Fine:** Not less than **₹1,00,000 (one lakh rupees)** [45, 64].

*(Note: An earlier iteration, the Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2001, also introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, contained an identical penal framework prescribing imprisonment for a term not less than three years and a fine of ₹1 lakh under its Clause 10 [41, 48]).*

Under **Clause 10** of the **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004**, any person who violates the provisions of the Act shall be punishable with:

### 1. WHAT IT IS
The **Computer Training Centres (Regulation) Bill, 2004** was introduced in the Lok Sabha as a Private Member's Bill by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi to regulate computer education centres across India [1, 2]. It mandates mandatory prior registration, prescription of uniform syllabi and fee structures, and penalties to curb instances of unregulated centres overcharging students or abruptly shutting down without completing courses [2, 3, 4].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
- **Proponent / Sponsoring Ministry:** Private Member's Bill introduced by Shri Iqbal Ahmed Saradgi, M.P. [1]. Executive regulatory powers under the proposed statute are assigned to the "appropriate Government" (Central Government or State Government) [1, 2].
- **Legal Status & Stage:** Introduced legislative proposal (Private Member's Bill) [1, 2]. It is not enacted law in force.
- **Date:** August 18, 2004 [2].

### 3. DESIGN (PENAL PROVISIONS)
Under **Clause 10** of the Bill, any person who violates the provisions of the proposed Act faces mandatory minimum statutory penalties [3]:

| Penalty Component | Stipulation under Clause 10 |
|---|---|
| **Minimum Term of Imprisonment** | Not less than **three years** [3] |
| **Minimum Fine** | Not less than **₹1,00,000** (one lakh rupees) [3] |

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
- **Arguments for (from Statement of Objects and Reasons):** Addresses rampant proliferation of unregistered computer centres charging exorbitant fees with inadequate facilities, preventing fly-by-night operators from abandoning enrolled students midway [2].
- **Arguments against / Concerns (Inference from text):** Imposes severe criminal liability (mandatory minimum 3-year imprisonment and ₹1 lakh fine) [3] without distinguishing administrative non-compliances from serious fraud, which creates high regulatory barriers and compliance risks for informal IT instructors.

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
- **Legislative Progression:** Track whether the Bill lapsed or was re-introduced in subsequent Lok Sabha sessions.
- **Subordinate Legislation:** Central Government's rule-making powers under Clause 11 for syllabus and fee standards [2, 3].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation and copying of computer programmes for debugging and operational use were addressed by amending Section 52(1) and Section 57 of the Copyright Act, 1957, establishing non-infringing fair-dealing exceptions and shielding lawful users from author moral-rights claims [2][3][8][17].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / In-charge:** Ministry of Human Resource Development (introduced by Shri Arjun Singh) [33].
* **Instrument:** Legislative Bill amending the Copyright Act, 1957 (Bill text stage; not enacted law at that point) [5].
* **Relevant Clauses:** Clause 17 (amending Section 52) and Clause 20 (amending Section 57) [2][8][17].

### 3. DESIGN & PROVISIONS
* **Insertion of Section 52(1)(aa):** Clause 17 of the Bill proposed inserting clause `(aa)` into sub-section (1) of Section 52 to provide that the following acts would not constitute an infringement of copyright [8]:
  * *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
    *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
    *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8].
* **Legislative Intent on "Debugging":** The Notes on Clauses clarify that proposed clause `(aa)` was specifically inserted to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner/possessor of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for "debugging" and to make back-up copies [3][7].
* **Protection Against Author's Special Rights (Section 57):** Clause 20 amended Section 57(1) of the principal Act by adding a proviso declaring that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause `(aa)` of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies [2][17]. This ensured that debugging adaptations would not be actionable as prejudicial distortions or modifications under the author's moral rights [2][17].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Proponents' Rationale:** Recognises the practical necessity for bona fide software users to adapt code to fix errors (debugging) and retain functioning systems without exposure to infringement or moral rights litigation [2][3].
* **Statutory Safeguards / Boundaries:** Computer programmes were simultaneously removed from the broader general fair-dealing exception for "private use" under Section 52(1)(a) to prevent unwarranted reproduction, confining adaptation and reproduction rights strictly to lawful possessors utilising the software for supplied purposes or temporary protection [3][8].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Follow-up Evolution:** Track subsequent legislative refinements to Section 52(1) regarding interoperability, reverse engineering, and observation/testing (later expanded in the Copyright Amendment Act, 1999) [14].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the proposed statutory mechanism to allow software adaptation for debugging purposes was introduced via an exception to copyright infringement under **Section 52(1)**, paired with a limiting proviso to the author's special moral rights under **Section 57** of the Copyright Act, 1957 [1][2][3].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Sponsor:** Ministry of Human Resource Development (introduced in the Lok Sabha by Arjun Singh, Minister of Human Resource Development) [4][5].
* **Instrument:** Legislative Bill (The Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992) [5][6].
* **Status in Record:** As-introduced text / proposed amendment [5][6].

### 3. DESIGN & PROVISIONS
The Bill proposed two linked provisions to enable and protect debugging and adaptation of computer programmes:

1. **Non-Infringement Exception — Proposed Section 52(1)(aa):**
   * Clause 17 of the Bill proposed inserting a new **clause (aa)** into sub-section (1) of Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957 [1][7].
   * This clause permitted:
     > *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
     > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
     > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [1].
   * As explained in the Notes on Clauses, this new clause was designed to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner/possessor of a copy to make adaptations for **"debugging"** and to create back-up copies [2][7].

2. **Consequential Proviso to Moral Rights — Proposed Section 57(1):**
   * Clause 20 sought to amend **Section 57(1)** (author's special rights to restrain or claim damages for distortion, mutilation, or modification) [3][8].
   * Consistent with the debugging proposal, it inserted an express proviso stating:
     > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [3][8].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Case For:** Recognised the practical necessity for bona fide software possessors to adapt and debug computer programmes so they can function as intended, while shielding them from infringement suits and moral-rights damage claims by authors [2][3][8].
* **Case Against / Restrictions:** Narrowed general private reproduction exceptions by excluding computer programmes from the general fair dealing scope of Section 52(1)(a) (to prevent unauthorised duplication), limiting the adaptation right strictly to lawful possessors utilising the programme for its supplied purpose [1][7].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Subsequent Evolution:** Subsequent statutory amendments (such as the Copyright (Amendment) Bill, 1999) introduced further clauses under Section 52(1) (e.g., clauses `(ab)`, `(ac)`, and `(ad)`) covering interoperability, observation/testing of principles, and non-commercial personal backup copies [9].

### WHAT IT IS
Under the **Copyright (Second Amendment) Bill, 1992**, the adaptation of a computer programme for debugging purposes was proposed to be permitted as an act not constituting copyright infringement through the insertion of a new **clause (aa)** in sub-section (1) of **Section 52** of the Copyright Act, 1957, complemented by a proviso to **Section 57** [2][3][8][17].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Introducing Authority:** Introduced in Lok Sabha by Arjun Singh, Minister of Human Resource Development, dated **6 May 1992** [11][29][33].
* **Instrument Type & Status:** Statutory amendment bill (as-introduced legislative text) [5].

### DESIGN
* **Section 52(1)(aa) Insertion:** The Bill proposed inserting clause `(aa)` into sub-section (1) of Section 52 to make non-infringing:
  > *"(aa) the making of copies of adaptation of a computer programme by the lawful possessor of a copy of such computer programme, from such copy—*
  > *(i) in order to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied; or*
  > *(ii) to make back-up copies purely as a temporary protection against loss, destruction or damage in order only to utilise the computer programme for the purpose for which it was supplied;"* [8].
* **Statutory Intent:** Notes on clauses explain that this clause was designed to cover the legitimate requirement of the lawful owner of a copy of a computer programme to make adaptations for **"debugging"** and to make back-up copies [3][7].
* **Author's Special Rights Exclusion (Section 57):** To protect users making such adaptations, Clause 20 of the Bill proposed a proviso to Section 57(1), barring the author from restraining or claiming damages for moral rights violations:
  > *"Provided that the author shall not have any right to restrain or claim damages in respect of any adaptation of a computer programme to which clause (aa) of sub-section (1) of section 52 applies."* [2][17].

### TRADE-OFFS
* **For User Adaptation & Interoperability:** Ensured bona fide, lawful possessors could adapt, debug, and run software to achieve operational utility without exposure to infringement suits or author moral-right claims [2][3][8][17].
* **Against Software Copyright Infringement:** Excluded computer programmes from the broader general "private use / private study" exemption of Section 52(1)(a) to prevent unauthorised reproduction, coupled with strict penalties under proposed Section 63C for knowing use of infringing software copies [3][8][13][21].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Successor Legislation:** Tracking the formal consolidation of these provisions into the enacted **Copyright (Amendment) Act, 1994** and subsequent refinements in the **Copyright (Amendment) Bill, 1999** (which introduced interoperability exceptions under Section 52(1)(ab)–(ad)) [4][14].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
The Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001 is a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S. S. Ahluwalia [1, 3] to provide free education (from school level up to post-graduate, medical, and technical education), free hostels, books, uniforms, and scholarships to the children of manual scavengers or Safai Karamcharis who were previously engaged in manually carrying human excreta [1, 2].

### 2. IDENTIFICATION RESPONSIBILITIES OF THE APPROPRIATE GOVERNMENT
Under **Clause 3** of the Bill, the statutory responsibility assigned to the appropriate Government regarding the identification of eligible beneficiaries encompasses the following specific duties:

* **Mandatory Survey:** It is the duty of the appropriate Government to conduct a survey within the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers [2].
* **Preparation of List:** It must prepare a list of such children, in such manner as may be prescribed, who are to be imparted education by such Government [2].
* **Periodic Revision:** It must cause the list of identified children to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [2].

*(Note: Under **Clause 2(a)**, the "appropriate Government" is defined as the State Government in the case of a State, and the Central Government in other cases [1]).*

### WHAT IT IS
Under **The Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** (introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S. S. Ahluwalia) [1, 2], the appropriate government is mandated to systematically survey and identify eligible children born of scavenger parents to impart free and comprehensive education [3, 4].

### IDENTIFICATION RESPONSIBILITIES (CLAUSE 3)
Under **Clause 3** ("Survey to be conducted by the appropriate Government") of the Bill as introduced [3]:

- **Conduct of Survey:** It is the duty of the appropriate government to conduct a survey in the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers [3].
- **Preparation of List:** The appropriate government must prepare a list of such children, in such manner as may be prescribed by rules, who are to be imparted education by that government [3].
- **Periodic Revision:** The appropriate government is required to cause the list to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed [3].

### RELEVANT STATUTORY DEFINITIONS
- **Appropriate Government (Clause 2(a)):** Means the Government of that State in the case of a State, and the Central Government in other cases [5].
- **Scavenger (Clause 2(e)):** Defined as a person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta before the commencement of the Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 [6].
- **Parent (Clause 2(c)):** In relation to any child of a scavenger, includes a guardian and every person having actual custody of the child [6].

### IMPLEMENTATION & OVERSIGHT MECHANISM
- **Attendance Authorities (Clause 7):** The appropriate government is empowered to appoint Attendance Authorities (and supporting personnel) to assist in discharging duties under the proposed Act [7].
- **Part-Time Education Exceptions (Clause 8):** If an Attendance Authority is satisfied that a child is unable to attend regular school due to economic or family circumstances, it may permit attendance at an approved part-time institution [8].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
The **Special Educational Facilities for Children of Manual Scavengers Bill, 2001** is a private member's legislative proposal introduced in the Rajya Sabha by Shri S.S. Ahluwalia [1, 2]. It seeks to mandate the provision of comprehensive, free educational facilities—ranging from school to post-graduate, medical, and technical education—along with boarding, uniforms, books, and scholarships to the children of individuals formerly engaged in manual scavenging [1, 3, 4].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Chamber / Stage:** Introduced in the Rajya Sabha (Bill No. LXX of 2001); private member's bill (as-introduced stage; not enacted law) [1, 2].
* **Responsible Authority:** The **appropriate Government**, defined under Clause 2(a) as the Government of a State in the case of a State, and the Central Government in other cases [1].

### 3. DESIGN: IDENTIFICATION OF ELIGIBLE BENEFICIARIES
Under **Clause 3** of the Bill, the responsibility assigned to the appropriate Government regarding the identification of beneficiaries is explicitly established as follows [3]:
* **Duty to Conduct Surveys:** It is the duty of the appropriate Government to conduct surveys within the area under its jurisdiction to find out the children of scavengers [3].
* **Preparation of Lists:** The appropriate Government is mandated to prepare a list of such children who are to be imparted education by the government, in such manner as may be prescribed [3].
* **Periodic Revision:** The appropriate Government must cause the list of eligible children to be revised at such intervals as may be prescribed by rules [3].
* **Statutory Definitions of Beneficiaries:** A "scavenger" is defined under Clause 2(e) as a person who had been engaged or employed for manually carrying human excreta before the commencement of the Employment of Manual Scavengers and Construction of Dry Latrines (Prohibition) Act, 1993 [3, 5].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Strongest Case For (Bill's Statement of Objects and Reasons):** Breaks the hereditary cycle of manual scavenging and systemic illiteracy by providing complete institutional and financial support for primary and higher education, directly removing root social and economic causes [2, 4].
* **Strongest Case Against / Fiscal Demands (Financial Memorandum):** Requires a recurring expenditure of about ₹100 crore per annum and a non-recurring expenditure of ₹10 crore from the Consolidated Fund of India, placing substantial logistical and identification burdens on state machinery to keep beneficiary registers accurately updated [6].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Appointment of Attendance Authorities:** Track whether administrative machinery and "Attendance Authorities" (empowered under Clause 7 to enforce attendance and oversee alternative schooling arrangements under Clause 8) are instituted alongside the survey mechanism [7, 8].
* **Rule-Making Execution:** Track rules framed under Clause 9 regarding the prescribed intervals and procedures for conducting surveys and revising beneficiary lists [8].

### WHAT IT IS
The **Right to Work Bill, 2002** was a Private Member's Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha by Shri G. M. Banatwalla to provide every adult citizen a legal right to appropriate work or an unemployment allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until work is provided [1, 4, 13]. To finance the allowance and fund administration, Section 9(1) directs the Central Government to establish the **Right to Work Fund** [1, 3, 4].

### OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
- **Proponent / Ministry Context:** Introduced as a Private Member's Bill by MP G. M. Banatwalla; the President's recommendation under Articles 117 and 274 was communicated via the Minister of Labour [4, 7].
- **Legal Status:** Introduced Bill (**Not in record** as enacted law).
- **Date:** Notice dated 27 February 2002; presidential recommendation dated 19 April 2002 [7, 9].

### DESIGN: SOURCES OF REVENUE CREDITED TO THE FUND
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Bill, the following five sources are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [1, 3]:

| Clause | Source of Revenue / Credit | Statutory Provision |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **(a)** | **Government Grants** | All grants made by the Central Government under Section 9(2) from time to time as required [1, 4]. |
| **(b)** | **Voluntary Donations** | All voluntary donations made to the Fund (which qualify for income-tax rebates/deductions under Section 11) [1, 2, 3]. |
| **(c)** | **Insurance Policy Contributions** | All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [1, 3]. |
| **(d)** | **Beneficiary Contributions** | All sums collected under Section 12 (mandatory contributions at a prescribed rate for a prescribed period from every citizen who secures work or a job after receiving work or allowance under the Act) [1, 3, 21]. |
| **(e)** | **Returns on Investments** | Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [3]. |

### TRADE-OFFS
- **Strongest Case in the Record:** Creates a multi-source self-replenishing mechanism (budgetary grants, tax-deductible donations, insurance contributions, and payroll-like paybacks from citizens once employed), which the Financial Memorandum projects would substantially reduce the central exchequer's net recurring burden over time [2, 33].
- **Strongest Case Against in the Record:** Places a recurring liability estimated at approximately ₹500 crore per annum initially on the Consolidated Fund of India to support the minimum statutory weekly unemployment allowance [33].

### IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
- **Subordinate Legislation Triggers:** Section 15(2) leaves key financial specifics to delegated rules, including the rate of allowance under Section 5, details of the Right to Work Insurance scheme under Section 10, income-tax rebate details under Section 11, and the contribution rates and periods under Section 12 [19].

Under **section 9(3)** of **The Right to Work Bill, 2002**, the following sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the **Right to Work Fund** [1], [2]:

1. **Government Grants:** All grants made by the Central Government under section 9(2) from time to time as may be required for the purposes of the Act [1].
2. **Voluntary Donations:** All voluntary donations made to the Fund [1], [2] (which, under section 11, qualify for income-tax rebates or deductions payable by the donee [2], [3]).
3. **Insurance Policy Contributions:** All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under section 10 [1], [2].
4. **Contributions from Employed Beneficiaries:** All sums collected under section 12 [1], [2] (which mandates that every citizen receiving work or an allowance under the Act contribute to the Fund at a prescribed rate for a prescribed period upon securing employment) [3].
5. **Returns on Investments:** Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [2].

### **WHAT IT IS**
The Right to Work Bill, 2002 was introduced as a private member's bill in the Lok Sabha by Shri G. M. Banatwalla to provide citizens with the legal right to work and an unemployment allowance (not less than ₹200 per week) until appropriate work is provided [4, 13]. To finance this allowance and associated administrative costs, Section 9(1) of the Bill mandates the establishment of the **Right to Work Fund** [1, 3].

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Ministry / Government:** Central Government [4].
* **Status / Version:** Introduced Bill (Lok Sabha Private Member's Bill, introduced in 2002; received Presidential recommendation under Articles 117 and 274 on 19 April 2002) [4, 7]. Not enacted into law.

### **DESIGN: MANDATED SOURCES OF REVENUE**
Under **Section 9(3)** of the Bill, the following five sources of revenue are mandated to be credited to the Right to Work Fund [1, 3]:

| Provision | Mandated Revenue Source |
|---|---|
| **Section 9(3)(a)** | All grants made by the Central Government under Section 9(2) from time to time as required for the purpose of the Act [1]. |
| **Section 9(3)(b)** | All voluntary donations made to the Fund [1] (qualifying for income-tax rebate/deductions under Section 11) [2, 3]. |
| **Section 9(3)(c)** | All contributions in respect of the Right to Work Insurance Policy under Section 10 [1, 3]. |
| **Section 9(3)(d)** | All sums collected under Section 12 [1, 3] (mandatory contributions from every citizen who receives work or allowance under the Act, payable at a prescribed rate for a prescribed period immediately upon securing work) [21]. |
| **Section 9(3)(e)** | Any interest, dividend, or other return on any investment made out of any part of the Fund [3]. |

### **TRADE-OFFS**
* **Strongest case for:** It establishes a self-replenishing, multi-stream financing mechanism—leveraging initial central grants alongside citizen clawback contributions upon employment, market insurance coverage, and tax-incentivised philanthropic donations—to reduce the state's net fiscal liability over time [2, 3, 33].
* **Strongest case against:** The Bill projected an initial recurring outlay of approximately ₹500 crore per annum from the Consolidated Fund of India [33], and imposing mandatory contributions on formerly unemployed workers immediately after securing employment could reduce take-home income for vulnerable job seekers [21].

### **IMPLEMENTATION WATCH**
* Track whether any future statutory employment guarantee models incorporate worker-repayment or mandatory social insurance contribution mechanisms similar to Sections 10 and 12 [3, 21].

Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004** (enacted as the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007) [17], Section 344K(f) defines what qualifies an entity to be a **"recognised security organisation"** [1], [2]:

### Qualifying Criteria
To qualify for designation and authorisation by the Central Government, an entity must be:
1. **Form of Entity:** "any organisation, company, firm or body of individuals" [1], [2];
2. **Expertise & Knowledge Requirements:**
   - Having **expertise in matters relating to security** [1], [2]; and
   - Having **knowledge of ship and port operations** [1], [2].

### Statutory Designation & Purpose
Such an entity qualifies to be authorised by the Central Government by **notification in the Official Gazette** to carry out [1], [2]:
- Assessment, verification, approval, or certification required under Part IXB of the Act or by the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code [2].

Additionally, the Central Government is empowered under Section 344M(2) to authorise any recognised security organisation to carry out security measures on its behalf subject to prescribed conditions [25].

### Statutory Qualification Criteria

Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004** (enacted as the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007) [1, 5], section 344K(f) defines a **"recognised security organisation"** as [1, 2]:

* **Form of Entity:** Any organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals [1, 2].
* **Substantive Qualifications & Capabilities:**
  * Must possess **expertise in matters relating to security** [1, 2]; and
  * Must possess **knowledge of ship and port operations** [1, 2].
* **Authorization & Function:** 
  * Must be authorized by the Central Government by **notification in the Official Gazette** [2];
  * Authorized to carry out **assessment, verification, approval, or certification** required by Part IXB or by the **International Ship and Port Facility Security Code** (ISPS Code) [2].

Additionally, under the proviso to section 344M(2), the Central Government may authorize any recognised security organisation to carry out security measures on its behalf, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed [3].

### **WHAT IT IS**
Under the **Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004** (enacted as the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Act, 2007, inserting Part IXB into the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958), a **"recognised security organisation"** is defined under proposed **Section 344K(f)** [1, 2]. To qualify for designation and authorisation by the Central Government, an entity must satisfy specific statutory qualifications [1, 2]:

* **Form of Entity:** It must be any organisation, company, firm, or body of individuals [1, 2].
* **Substantive Expertise & Knowledge:** It must possess:
  1. Expertise in matters relating to security [1, 2]; and
  2. Knowledge of ship and port operations [1, 2].
* **Government Authorisation:** It must be authorised by the Central Government by notification in the Official Gazette to carry out assessment, verification, approval, or certification required by Part IXB or by the International Ship and Port Facility Security (ISPS) Code [1, 2].

### **OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS**
* **Owning Ministry / Authority:** Central Government (Ministry of Shipping, Road Transport and Highways / designated authority) [2, 3].
* **Legal Instrument:** Proposed insertion of Section 344K into Part IXB of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 via the Merchant Shipping (Amendment) Bill, 2004 (introduced in Lok Sabha on **23 December 2004**; passed Lok Sabha on **14 August 2007**; passed Rajya Sabha on **6 September 2007**; received Presidential Assent on **24 September 2007** as Act No. 40 of 2007) [1, 5, 17].
* **Statutory vs Executive:** Statutory enactment empowering the executive to issue notifications and prescribe operational conditions [2, 25].

### **DESIGN & FUNCTIONS**
* **Primary Mandate:** Authorised to carry out assessment, verification, approval, or certification required under Part IXB or by the ISPS Code [2].
* **Delegated Security Measures:** Under the proviso to proposed **Section 344M(2)**, the Central Government is empowered to authorise any recognised security organisation to carry out any of the security measures under Section 344M on its behalf, subject to such conditions as may be prescribed [25].

### **TRADE-OFFS**
* **Case For:** Enables compliance with the mandatory International Maritime Organisation (IMO) ISPS Code under SOLAS 1974, leveraging specialised private/technical bodies to handle technical assessments and certification without which Indian vessels would face entry barriers abroad and foreign ships could not call at Indian ports [5, 34].
* **Case Against / Regulatory Burden:** Imposes prescriptive compliance costs and operational oversight requirements across ports and shipping operators, delegating critical national security verification functions to non-governmental organisations and firms [2, 25].

### **IMPLEMENTATION WATCH**
* **Gazette Notifications:** Publication of specific Central Government notifications authorising designated organisations to perform assessments and certifications [2].
* **Subordinate Legislation:** Framing of rules under proposed Section 344T and conditions under Section 344M regarding the exact scope and limitations placed on recognised security organisations [11, 25].

### 1. WHAT IT IS
Under the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004, the standard workday duration considered when fixing piece-rate wage schedules for unskilled labourers is **seven hours** [1]. The statutory framework stipulates that where wages are directly linked to the quantity of work performed, the schedule of rates fixed by the State Government must enable a person working seven hours to normally earn a wage equal to the statutory wage rate [1].

### 2. OWNERSHIP & LEGAL STATUS
* **Ministry / Jurisdiction:** Ministry of Rural Development (Central Government oversight; implementation by State Governments, State Employment Guarantee Councils, and Panchayats) [2, 3].
* **Instrument Type:** Statutory legislation (enacted as The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005 / Act No. 42 of 2005) [4].
* **Date & Stage:** Received the assent of the President on **5 September 2005** [4].

### 3. DESIGN
* **Workday Standard & Piece-Rate Baseline:** When wages are tied to output, rates are paid according to the schedule of rates fixed annually by the State Government in consultation with the State Council [1]. Under Schedule I, paragraph 8, the schedule of rates for unskilled labourers must be fixed so that a person working for **seven hours** normally earns a wage equal to the applicable wage rate [1].
* **Wage Floor Guarantee:** Under no circumstances may labourers be paid less than the statutory wage rate [1]. Under section 6, the Central Government specifies the wage rate (not less than **₹60 per day**), or until fixed, the minimum wage determined by the State Government for agricultural labourers under section 3 of the Minimum Wages Act, 1948 applies [5].

### 4. TRADE-OFFS
* **Pro-Worker Productivity Protection:** Calibrating piece rates to a 7-hour workday protects workers from excessive physical exertion and prevents task-norm inflation that would otherwise depress real daily earnings below statutory minimum wage floors [1].
* **Fiscal & Output Risk:** Setting piece rates around a standard 7-hour norm requires precise, objective local task-rate schedules; misaligned soil or terrain output standards can either escalate programme wage outlays or trigger measurement disputes at worksites [1, 5].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Schedule Revision Tracking:** Periodic annual notifications issued by State Governments in consultation with State Employment Guarantee Councils specifying piece-rate task charts [1].
* **Disbursement Timeframes:** Verification that weekly or fortnightly disbursement timelines (mandated within 14 days of work completion) are strictly met [2].

### WHAT IT IS

The legislation broadens the statutory jurisdiction of the 1934 Act to include foreign-registered aircraft operating in or over Indian airspace and non-citizen operators residing or conducting business in India [14, 19], brings air traffic management and satellite-based navigation under statutory regulation [15, 22], establishes regulatory safety oversight powers, and sharply escalates penal deterrence across civil aviation offences [7, 11].

* **Administration & Safety Oversight (Section 4 / New Section 4A)**: Expressly empowers the **Director-General of Civil Aviation (DGCA)** or any officer specially empowered by the Central Government to execute **safety oversight functions** under the Act and rules [14, 32].
* **Expansion of Territorial & Entity Scope (Section 2 / Section 1(2))**: Extends the principal Act's application to:
  * Foreign-registered aircraft and persons on board when in or over India (Section 1(2)(c)) [2, 14].
  * Aircraft operated by non-citizens whose principal place of business or permanent residence is in India (Section 1(2)(d)) [14, 32].
* **Expanded Rule-Making & Oversight Powers (Section 5 / Section 5(2))**: Inserts clauses allowing the Central Government to formulate rules for:
  * Licensing of personnel engaged in **air traffic control (ATC)** (clause *ga*) [15, 39].
  * Certification, inspection, and regulation of communication, navigation, surveillance, or air traffic management (CNS/ATM) facilities (clause *gb*) [15, 39].
  * Mandatory safeguards protecting civil aviation against **acts of unlawful interference** and ensuring civil aviation security (clause *gc*) [15, 39].

  * **Section 5A**: Expands DGCA power to issue directions directly covering CNS/ATM operations, aerodrome maintenance, air traffic control, and civil aviation security [9, 39].

| Section Amended | Nature of Violation | Revised Statutory Penalty |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |

| **Section 10(1A)** | Carriage of arms/explosives, furnishing false information, or abetment | Imprisonment up to **3 years**, or fine up to **₹10 lakh**, or both (increased from 1 year or ₹2,000) [7, 69] |

| **Section 11** | Wilfully flying aircraft causing danger to person or property | Imprisonment up to **2 years**, or fine up to **₹10 lakh**, or both (increased from 6 months or ₹1,000) [7, 42] |
| **Section 11A** | Flying over prohibited areas / failure to head directions | Imprisonment increased from 6 months to **2 years** [41, 42] |
| **Section 11B(1)** | Failure to comply with building/obstacle directions near aerodromes (Section 9A) | Imprisonment up to **2 years**, or fine up to **₹10 lakh**, or both (increased from 6 months or ₹1,000) [7, 41] |

* **Case For (Institutional Record)**: Crucial modernisation closing regulatory vacuums arising from private airline operations, aerodrome privatisaion, shift from ground-based to satellite-based CNS/ATM technology, and compliance obligations under ICAO/Chicago Convention standards [11, 20, 22]. Escalated penalties deter critical security non-compliance and obstacle encroachments [7].

### 1. WHAT IT IS

  - Passed by the **Lok Sabha** on **2 August 2000** [2].
  - Passed with amendments by the **Rajya Sabha** on **11 August 2000** [2].
  - Amendments agreed to by the **Lok Sabha** on **11 August 2000** [2].
  - Received Presidential Assent on **25 August 2000** as **Act No. 30 of 2000** [2, 25].

---

### 3. DESIGN

#### Key Objectives and Components
- **Territorial Demarcation (Clauses 3 & 4):** Creates the State of Jharkhand comprising specified districts from the existing State of Bihar (including Bokaro, Chatra, Deoghar, Dhanbad, Dumka, Garhwa, Giridih, Godda, Gumla, Hazaribagh, Kodarma, Lohardaga, Pakur, Palamau, Ranchi, Sahebganj, Singhbhum East, and Singhbhum West); residuary territories remain with the State of Bihar [23, 24].

- **Legislative Apportionment (Part III):** Allocates sitting members and outlines delimitation procedures for parliamentary and assembly constituencies between Bihar and Jharkhand [2, 4].
- **Apportionment of Assets and Liabilities (Part VI, Clause 41):** Provides that successor States receive benefits and bear financial liabilities arising out of decisions taken by the predecessor State, subject to equitable financial adjustments [37, 39]. Population ratio between residuary Bihar and Jharkhand is fixed based on the 1991 Census as **645.30 : 218.44** [11, 15, 16].
- **Distribution of Revenues (Clause 40):** The President determines the revenue shares of Bihar and Jharkhand from amounts payable to the predecessor State based on the recommendations of the Finance Commission under Article 280 [5, 8, 37].

- **Adaptation of Laws (Clauses 84 & 85):** Existing laws remain applicable within their territorial scope; appropriate governments are given powers to adapt, modify, or repeal laws within two years from the appointed day [8, 17, 18].

- **Central Government:** Issues notifications appointing the "appointed day" [1, 6], directs administrative boards, resolves jurisdictional disputes (e.g., Clause 81) [7], and exercises statutory adaptation powers for Union List subjects [17].
- **Successor State Governments:** Administer their respective state jurisdictions, local administrative reorganisations (Clause 6) [24], and adaptations of State List laws [17].
- **Dedicated Development Unit:** The Central Government established a dedicated unit in the Planning Commission under the direct charge of the Deputy Chairman to focus on the economic development of residuary Bihar [16, 25].

#### Penalties
- **Penalties:** **Not in record.** The Bill and its legal/miscellaneous clauses (Clauses 83 to 92) contain administrative, transitional, and legal adaptation provisions adapted from the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, and specify no standalone penal code offences or criminal penalty schedules [3, 5, 7].

- **Strongest Case For:** Directly addresses the long-standing democratic and regional aspirations of the people of the Jharkhand region for self-governance and focused development [16, 25].

### 3. DESIGN & KEY CLAUSES
* **Offence of Money-Laundering (Section 3):** Whosoever directly or indirectly attempts to indulge, knowingly assists, is knowingly a party to, or is actually involved in any process or activity connected with the proceeds of crime and projecting it as untainted property is guilty of the offence [14, 19].
* **Obligations of Banking Companies & Intermediaries (Sections 12–15):** Requires banking companies, financial institutions, and intermediaries to maintain and furnish information on reportable transactions in the manner prescribed by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India [18, 26].
* **Investigation, Search, and Arrest (Sections 16–24):** Empowers the Director and authorized subordinate officers to conduct surveys, carry out searches of premises/vessels/vehicles/aircraft, break open locks, seize property/records, execute arrests, retain property/records, and establishes rules regarding the burden of proof [26, 27].
* **Attachment and Confiscation (Chapter III & Special Courts):** Establishes an Adjudicating Authority (Section 6) to adjudicate attachments, designates Sessions Courts as Special Courts (Section 43) for trial and confiscation proceedings, and creates an Appellate Tribunal (Section 25) [10, 14, 24].
* **Cross-Border Reciprocal Arrangements:** Includes mechanisms for reciprocal arrangements to facilitate the transfer of funds kept outside India, confiscation, and extradition of accused persons [10, 22].

### 4. PENALTIES
* **General Sentence (Section 4):** Rigorous imprisonment for a minimum term of **3 years**, extendable up to **7 years**, along with a fine of up to **₹5 lakh** [14, 19].
* **Aggravated Drug-Related Offences (Section 4 Proviso):** Where the proceeds of crime relate to offences specified under Paragraph 2 of Part A of the Schedule, the maximum term of rigorous imprisonment extends up to **10 years** [19].
* **Non-Compliance Penalties:** Empowers the Director to levy fines on any banking company, financial institution, or intermediary failing to comply with reporting and record-maintenance requirements under Section 12 [26].

### 5. IMPLEMENTATION WATCH
* **Notification of Commencement:** Tracking Central Government gazette notifications for bringing individual provisions and sections into force [10, 24].
* **Operationalisation of Authorities:** Tracking the formal appointment and constitution of the Adjudicating Authority (Section 6), the Appellate Tribunal (Section 25), and designated Special Courts (Section 43) [10, 14, 24].
* **Reporting Rulemaking:** Tracking rules framed jointly with the Reserve Bank of India specifying threshold limits, procedures, and modalities of disclosure for financial intermediaries [18, 26].
